reference.source: Swaiman's Pediatric Neurology / ILAE nonepileptic paroxysmal disorders
clinicalPearls: A benign non-epileptic paroxysmal disorder of infancy that mimics epileptic spasms (West syndrome) but occurs with a normal EEG and normal development
Onset is usually within the first year (commonly 3-9 months) with spontaneous resolution typically before 2 years of age
Episodes comprise brief clusters of myoclonic-like jerks, spasms, shudders, head nodding or tonic posturing of the neck, trunk and arms, often while awake and sometimes during feeding or excitement
Consciousness is preserved throughout and the infant remains alert and interactive during and immediately after episodes
The interictal and ictal EEG are normal with no hypsarrhythmia, which is the key distinction from West syndrome and other epileptic encephalopathies
Development and neurological examination remain normal and there is no regression
Diagnosis is clinical, strongly supported by video-EEG capturing typical events without an electrographic correlate
No treatment is required, but West syndrome must be actively excluded because it demands urgent therapy; recognition prevents unnecessary antiepileptic or hormonal treatment
reference.pathophysiology: The cause is unknown; this is a non-epileptic, self-limiting phenomenon presumed to reflect transient immaturity of motor control in the developing brain, possibly involving subcortical (basal ganglia and brainstem) motor pathways. The complete absence of any EEG correlate confirms that the events are not cortical epileptic seizures. The disorder resolves as neurological maturation proceeds and overlaps clinically with shuddering attacks and other benign non-epileptic spasms within the same spectrum described by Fejerman.
additionalDifferentials: West syndrome or epileptic (infantile) spasms with hypsarrhythmia
Other early infantile epilepsies such as myoclonic epilepsy of infancy
Shuddering attacks, which may be part of the same spectrum
Benign neonatal or infantile sleep myoclonus
Tonic reflux posturing (Sandifer syndrome) and spasmus nutans
additionalInvestigations: Video-EEG, ideally capturing an episode, demonstrating a normal ictal and interictal record
Review of home video of typical events
Serial developmental assessment confirming normal progress
Neurological examination confirming normal tone and milestones
MRI brain only if the examination is abnormal or the diagnosis is uncertain
Metabolic screen reserved for atypical or regressive presentations
redFlags: Developmental stagnation or regression suggesting an epileptic encephalopathy
Hypsarrhythmia or any epileptiform abnormality on EEG
Abnormal neurological examination or dysmorphic features
Episodes with impaired awareness or an evolving pattern
Persistence beyond the expected age or increasing frequency and severity
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent; it is a benign self-limiting condition that resolves spontaneously by around 2 years of age with a normal neurodevelopmental outcome.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as West syndrome, or missing West syndrome by assuming benignity, when a normal EEG is essential to differentiate them
Failing to arrange video-EEG, risking either missed epilepsy or unnecessary treatment
Starting antiepileptic drugs or hormonal therapy for a benign condition
Not monitoring development, which is the key discriminator from an epileptic encephalopathy
Confusing the episodes with gratification behaviour or reflux posturing
